summary: Describes a tag for labeling the language of information, how to register values, and how to match tags. It is a Best Current Practice. It was replaced by RFC 4646 and RFC 4647.

eli5.summary: Tags such as en or fr tell a computer which language a text uses. This explains how those tags are built and matched. Newer documents later replaced it.

questions: how to register a language tag
subtitle: How short tags such as en or en-US label the language of content, and how new tags get registered.

tldr.problem: Software that shows, speaks, spell-checks or prints information needs to know which human language it is in, and needs a common way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: A language tag is a primary subtag (often an ISO 639 code) followed by optional subtags such as an ISO 3166 country code, joined by hyphens, with an IANA process for registering other tags and a prefix rule for matching.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3066 replaced RFC 1766 and has itself been obsoleted by RFC 4646 and RFC 4647.

today: RFC 3066 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 47) that is now obsolete: it was replaced by RFC 4646 and RFC 4647. It had itself replaced RFC 1766.

sections.title: Why Label Languages
sections.content:
Information is often available in more than one language, and tools such as dictionaries can help with a language. Many kinds of processing also need to know the language: spell-checking, computer-synthesized speech, Braille and high-quality print rendering.

RFC 3066 specifies an identifier mechanism (the language tag), a registration function for values of that identifier, and a construct for matching against those values. It is BCP 47 and obsoletes RFC 1766.
sections.eli5: If a book is labeled with its language, a reader or a talking computer knows what to expect before opening it.

sections.title: Tag Syntax and Sources
sections.content:
A tag is a primary subtag of 1 to 8 letters followed by any number of subtags of 1 to 8 letters or digits, each joined by a hyphen. Tags are case insensitive. Capitalization conventions exist (country codes in capitals, language codes in lower case) but carry no meaning.

The first subtag is interpreted by its length. Two-letter subtags follow ISO 639, three-letter subtags follow ISO 639 part 2, i is reserved for IANA-defined registrations and x is reserved for private use. A two-letter second subtag is an ISO 3166 alpha-2 country code. Second subtags of 3 to 8 letters may be registered with IANA, and there are no rules beyond syntax for later subtags.

Tags built wholly from these assigned codes need no IANA registration. Examples in the text include en-US, en-scouse and sgn-US-MA. The ISO 3166 user-assigned codes AA, QM-QZ, XA-XZ and ZZ MUST NOT be used to form language tags.
sections.eli5: A tag is like a name with parts: first the language, then maybe the country or the local style, joined by dashes, such as en-US.

sections.title: Choosing and Interpreting a Tag
sections.content:
When several tags could describe the same text, interoperability is best if everyone uses the same one. The RFC sets rules: use the most precise tagging known that is useful, MUST use the ISO 639-1 two-character code when one exists, MUST prefer the ISO tag over an IANA-registered i- tag, and SHOULD NOT use UND (Undetermined) or MUL (Multiple) when omitting the tag or listing several languages is possible.

A tag always denotes a language used by humans to communicate. Programming languages are explicitly excluded. Tags that share a prefix are not guaranteed to be mutually intelligible, and what the tag means for a document is defined by the standard for the context it appears in. In markup such as HTML and XML, language can be attached to each part of a document, for example a French span inside a Norwegian document.
sections.eli5: Everybody should use the same label for the same language. The labels are only for languages people speak, not computer languages.

sections.title: Language Ranges and Matching
sections.content:
A language-range has the same syntax as a language tag, or is the single asterisk character. A range matches a tag if it exactly equals the tag, or exactly equals a prefix of the tag such that the first character after the prefix is a hyphen. So the range en matches en-US. The asterisk range matches any tag, although a protocol may add rules: HTTP/1.1 says it matches only languages not matched by another range in an Accept-Language header.

The RFC cautions that prefix matching does not imply that a user who understands one tag also understands every tag it prefixes. The rule simply allows prefix tags to be used when that is true.
sections.eli5: If you say you read 'en', you are happy with 'en-US' and other tags that start with 'en-'. A star means 'anything'.

sections.title: Registering Tags with IANA
sections.content:
Anyone who wants a tag not given an interpretation in section 2.2 and not already registered MUST use the registration procedure. The requester fills in a form giving name, e-mail, the tag, the English and native names of the language, a reference to a published description and any other information.

The form is sent to a mailing list for a 2-week review. A language tag reviewer, appointed by the IETF Applications Area Director, then forwards it to IANA or rejects it because of significant objections raised publicly. Rejected applications can be revised and resubmitted, which restarts the 2-week period, and reviewer decisions can be appealed to the IESG.

Registrations are never deleted. A tag that should no longer be used is amended with a remark such as DEPRECATED.
sections.eli5: If you need a new label, you fill in a form, people get two weeks to comment, and then a reviewer decides. Labels are never erased, only marked as old.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The one security issue raised since RFC 1766 is that language ranges used in content negotiation may reveal the nationality of the sender and so identify potential targets for surveillance. The RFC calls this a special case of the general fact that anything you send is visible to the receiver. Judging the threat and any countermeasures is left to each application protocol.

On character sets, tags use only the characters A-Z, a-z, 0-9 and HYPHEN-MINUS, so presenting them should not cause character set problems.
sections.eli5: Telling a website which languages you read can hint at where you are from, so be aware of what the label gives away.
